eyebrow: In development · built in public on Solana devnet
headline: The first trade is in flight.
lede: dClutch is a protocol for fully collateralized markets on real-world numbers — every claim backed one-for-one by collateral locked up before the claim exists. It is being built in public, on Solana's devnet, and this page is the live edge: what is being worked on right now, in plain words, with real numbers.

stats.detail: each founded atomically — five stages, one transaction; the one founding right now is the first that will be able to switch trading on

statsProvenance: Hand-written from the run logs and the commit trail, not read live from the chain — the date above is the promise. The front page's numbers are the live ones.

now.title: A new flagship market is founding on devnet
now.detail: An ~85-transaction campaign is running against the live cluster right now. It ends in one atomic transaction that locks the collateral machinery, founds the market, wires settlement, and opens the doors — and this is the first market in the protocol's history whose release carries its own trading switch.

now.title: The first capability activation in the protocol's history
now.detail: Every market opened before today was born with its trading switch missing — open, but permanently silent. The component that flips the switch was written this morning and proven against the protocol's real evaluators before being allowed anywhere near a live chain. It executes the moment the founding above finalizes.

now.title: The first trade
now.detail: Two participants get admitted with real (worthless, devnet) collateral, and one buys a claim from the other — the first trade this protocol will ever clear. By the time you read this it may already have happened: this page is updated by hand, and reality runs ahead of it, never behind.

recent.title: The first atomic founding
recent.detail: For most of this protocol's life, creating a market took a ladder of separate transactions that could die half-way. Now it is one transaction — five stages, all-or-nothing, squeezed under Solana's per-transaction compute ceiling. If any stage fails, the market never existed.

recent.title: A market on a public chain, with people in it
recent.detail: The flagship market was founded on devnet in an 82-transaction campaign, every step finalized and verified against two independent RPC providers — and then two participants were admitted and collateral-funded, 700 units each.

recent.title: The founding machinery stopped caring what kind of market you found
recent.detail: Four different families of market logic have now crossed the same selection machinery — one of them with zero changes to the shared path, which is the proof. One founding pipeline, any market family: that is the point of the design.

recent.title: Every lamport accounted for
recent.detail: The first whole-market money statement traced 596.7 million of 597.1 million lamports across 121 accounts — then decomposed the missing 385,000 exactly rather than shrugging: four recorded-but-uncounted journals plus one named fee. Found along the way: 78% of what a founding pays is rent on permanent public records.

recent.title: A load simulator, tested and waiting
recent.detail: A traffic generator that trades against a live market in sustained cycles, checkpointing so it can be killed and resumed byte-identically. Seventeen tests green. It flips to the real devnet market with one config edit, the moment there is a trade to imitate.

recent.title: A site that is not allowed to lie
recent.detail: This site ships with 783 tests, and some exist only to pin honesty: the front page may not promise that you can trade on a market until trading is actually possible, may not show an unread value as a zero, and may not carry a sentence that rots as time passes.

walls.intro: When a defect stops the whole line, it gets a number, a root cause, and a one-line epitaph — in public, in the evidence ledger. Twenty-two so far. A few of the fallen:

entries.name: Wall 4 · the off-by-one frame
entries.epitaph: Two programs read the same list of accounts from two different starting points. The refusal was forty accounts deep; the fix was one offset.

entries.name: Wall 6 · the check nobody could satisfy
entries.epitaph: A guard equated a signer with a vault. It was born two days earlier with zero test fixtures, so every test that could have caught it was green.

entries.name: Wall 7 · the digest named for its hopes
entries.epitaph: A hash field was named for where its bytes were hoped to come from, not for what they actually hash. It misled two independent debugging efforts in one morning. Standing rule since: digests are named for what they hash.

entries.name: Wall 8 · the compute ceiling
entries.epitaph: The atomic founding executed every stage and ran out of gas at the last door. Decoding one cache once per batch instead of once per role bought back 228,000 units.

entries.name: Wall 10 · refusing our own success
entries.epitaph: A market opened, and the tooling refused to believe it — there was no branch for the exact success it had just produced. The most honest bug of the week.

entries.name: Wall 22 · the missing switch
entries.epitaph: No market in the protocol's history could actually switch trading on — the part that does it had never been built. It exists now, proven against the real evaluators, and is being installed on a live market as you read this.

closing: All of this is on Solana's devnet, a public test network whose tokens are worthless by construction. There is no token, nothing for sale, and no value at risk anywhere. What is being built is the machinery — and you can watch it run.
